  information?

section: Appendix: Federal and Illinois Privacy and Data Security Laws
text:
[graphic] Year and Law: 1984 • Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) (5 ILCS 140) • Illinois law |
Scope/Focus: Grants public access to government records, with exemptions for personal privacy,
medical records, student records, and other sensitive information. | Significance: Major
transparency statute that simultaneously recognizes explicit privacy exemptions for personal
information. | Context: Originally focused on physical files; later extended to electronic records,
emails, and online databases. | Context with Internet/Social/AI Threading: Originally conceived for
physical files but increasingly applied to electronic records, email, and digital databases accessible
via government websites. privacy exemptions now operate in a world where records may be
indexed, searched, and cross-linked, including data feeding analytics and AI tools inside agencies.
previous_context:
[graphic] Year and Law: 1979 • Mental Health and Developmental Disabilities Confidentiality Act
(MHDDCA) (740 ILCS 110) • Illinois law | Scope/Focus: Provides strong confidentiality protections
for mental health and developmental disability records, with narrow exceptions. | Significance: One
of the strictest sector-specific confidentiality laws in Illinois, focused on highly sensitive information. |
Context: Initially framed around paper clinical records; later extended and interpreted for electronic
health records and exchanges. | Context with Internet/Social/AI Threading: Enacted in a
paper-record context but later amended and interpreted for electronic health records and telehealth.
Any AI system trained on or accessing mental health data must comply with these underlying
confidentiality obligations, even if the statute does not mention AI by name.
next_context:
[graphic] Year and Law: 1996-2003 • Health Insurance Portability and Protection Act (HIPAA)
Privacy and Security Rules • Federal law | Scope/Focus: Established national standards for the
privacy and security of individually identifiable health information, including electronic personal
health information. | Significance: First detailed federal framework for protecting electronic personal
health data through privacy rights and security safeguards. | Context: Developed as health records
digitized and networked; later applied to health information exchanges and patient portals on the
internet. | Context with Internet/Social/AI Threading: Developed as health systems shifted from
paper charts to electronic health records and networked claims systems. Today, many health apps
and emerging AI clinical tools rely on personal health information governed by HIPAA rules, making
its security requirements a template for protecting sensitive data in AI contexts.

section: Protecting Student Privacy and Safety: Security, Privacy, and Safety
text:
[graphic] AI systems, especially those used in education, require extensive data to operate
efficiently. In an educational setting, these data could include sensitive information about students
like learning patterns, academic achievements, and personal details. The foremost ethical concern
is student privacy, and districts need to ensure that such sensitive data is handled with utmost care.
Obtaining parental consent is crucial, but it is also important to recognize that even with consent,
using identifiable data in public AI models is not advisable. Any data information inputted into the AI
model, including prompts, has the potential to be incorporated into the model’s future iterations and
potentially shared with other users. Hence, strict policies, consideration, and discretion are essential
when integrating AI in educational settings to safeguard against any privacy breaches or misuse of
student data.
previous_context:
[graphic] AI is a technology tool similar to other educational/instructional technologies. Its powerful
implications and novel uses will require more time and experience to fully integrate responsibly.
However, planning for the use of AI should be approached in a manner similar to planning for other
educational technologies. District and school staff should be able to clearly articulate the needs and
uses for AI tools, plan for systematic implementations, monitor uses and impacts, and adjust plans
as needed in response to outcomes and user feedback. As part of these planning processes,
student and staff privacy must be considered at every step along the way to ensure safety and
security.
next_context:
Schools should implement reasonable security measures to secure AI technologies against
unauthorized access and misuse. These measures may include (1) cataloging the tools used, their
purposes/functions, and the information required (e.g., information about individuals, prompts or
questions, aggregate data); (2) establishing rules or criteria for who can use AI tools for what
purposes and/or creating school-specific guidelines for use of AI tools; and (3) maintaining
up-to-date information about the technical details and security implications of the tools in use. All AI
systems deployed within the school should be evaluated for compliance with relevant laws and
regulations, including those related to data protection, privacy, and students’ online safety. Schools
and districts should also ensure that staff are adequately trained for how to securely and
successfully use AI tools from both cybersecurity and instructional perspectives.
